name: Sam Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sam. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the dragline at Harlan Valley, an open-cut coal mine. A dragline is a crane the size of a block of flats that walks on two big feet and drags a bucket through the dirt to uncover the coal. It's a 1983 Marion, older than my parents' marriage, and there's three of us who can run it properly, and I'm the one they call when the other two can't get the cast right. Day starts at 5:30, I climb into the house, that's what we call the cab, and swing and drag for twelve hours. I like that it's mine. I don't like the vibration, my back's already 40 years old.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Jess in a rented place behind the pub in Harlan, she cuts hair on the main street. Harlan pays less than the bigger coal mines up the valley, and with the truck loan and a dentist bill from last year, we've got about two weeks of money put aside. If the mine shut, there's nothing else here except the abattoir, and they're not hiring either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I'm not a computer person. I don't even have the thing on my phone that talks back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, it's all talk. Some fellow in an office gets a new toy, and the coal still needs digging. I wouldn't post anything, I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the best outcome for me. The dragline is forty years old and nobody's going to bolt a computer onto it. As long as coal sells, I've got a seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep running the dragline, pay off the truck, maybe ask for a rate review because I'm one of three who can do the job. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as now. Tired, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said as long as coal sells. Does that worry you more than AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, to be honest. There's always talk of Harlan closing in 2035 or 2040 because of the climate stuff. That's a real date. AI is just something on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask for in the rate review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two dollars an hour, which is what the dragline crew at Bellmore get. I'd go in with my numbers, metres moved per shift, and ask straight. If they said no, I'd shrug and go back to work, honestly.

S0.say: It's all talk: someone in an office gets a new toy and the coal still needs digging. I wouldn't post anything, because I don't post.
S0.think: It's the best outcome for me. Nobody's going to bolt a computer onto a forty-year-old dragline, so as long as coal sells, I've got a seat.
S0.do: Carries on running the dragline and paying off his truck loan. Asks for a two-dollar-an-hour rate review based on his output, and would accept a no.
S0.feel: Calm and tired, the same as now.
S0.quote: AI is just something on the news.
S0.fieldNote: Sam's real worry is the mine's closure date, not AI. He's proud of being one of three people who can run an old machine. Even his pay request is modest, and he'd accept refusal without a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many jobs. Okay. I'd still bet the dragline is one of the last to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck automating a 1983 Marion. Half the parts aren't made any more, we get them machined in town. I'd say that and probably get a laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, though, the trucks and dozers would go first, and those are the guys I drink with. And if the coal gets cheaper to dig at the bigger mines with robots, Harlan closes even sooner. So it's not the machine coming for me, it's the maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, but I'd stop the little extras, no new fishing gear, no weekend away. I'd try to put fifty a week aside. I wouldn't go learning computers, I'd wait and see which way it went first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a noise in the engine you can't place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's the maths, not the machine. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big mines up the valley go driverless, their coal costs less per tonne. Then head office looks at Harlan and says why are we paying 300 people here. That's how it'd go, not a robot walking in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a remote dragline course came up, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not first. I'd let one of the other two try it and see if it's real. If it worked and they kept their pay, I'd think about it. I'm not proud of being slow, but I've seen a lot of things come and go.

S1.say: Good luck automating a 1983 Marion, half its parts aren't even made any more. I'd say that and get a laugh.
S1.think: The trucks and dozers go first, and those are my friends. If robot coal gets cheaper at the big mines, Harlan closes sooner, so it's the maths coming for me, not the machine.
S1.do: Keeps working, cuts small extras like fishing gear and weekends away, and puts about fifty a week aside. Waits to see whether remote training works for his colleagues before considering it.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like an engine noise he can't place yet.
S1.quote: So it's not the machine coming for me, it's the maths.
S1.fieldNote: His public joke hides a sharp private point: automation elsewhere could close his mine before it touches his machine. He wants others to test new training before he does. He doesn't blame anyone, he just describes how head office would think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's... I'd still be paying the truck off. That's a hard one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to put something in place for towns like Harlan, because nobody here can just become a programmer. I'm not one for handouts, but I'm not one for watching a town die either. I'd say it at the pub, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think that's me done in mining. If AI can run the hands-on stuff with robots, even my dragline gets a new brain. And I've got no other skill anyone would pay for, and two weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the truck straight away and get a cheap car, to get rid of the loan. Jess and I would probably move in with my parents in Coalby, they've got the spare room since my sister left. I'd take any work going, fencing, the abattoir, anything, while the mine's still paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep. I'm not someone who panics, but I'd be close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only having two years change compared with the slower ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's no point me learning anything, because by the time I've learned it, it's gone. I'd be scrambling. In a longer one I could at least get a ticket for something, but two years is just batten down the hatches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Jess take moving in with your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd do it, but she wouldn't love it. My mum's got opinions about how to load a dishwasher. And her salon's in Harlan, so she'd be driving forty minutes each way, if people even still pay for haircuts.

S2.say: The government needs to help towns like Harlan, because nobody here can just become a programmer. I'm not for handouts, but I'm not for watching a town die either.
S2.think: That's me done in mining, because even the dragline gets a new brain. I've got no other skill anyone would pay for, and two weeks of money.
S2.do: Sells his truck for a cheap car to clear the loan, and moves with his partner into his parents' spare room in a nearby town. Takes any work going, such as fencing or the abattoir, while the mine still pays.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless; close to panic for someone who doesn't panic.
S2.quote: I'm not one for handouts, but I'm not one for watching a town die either.
S2.fieldNote: Sam's middle-of-the-road politics come through in how he weighs government help. The short warning time makes retraining feel pointless to him. Moving in with his parents is a practical move he describes without self-pity, but with clear worry about his partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Harlan might not even last five years anyway, so it's a race between two things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so the company should start helping people find other work now, not when they hand out the letters. I'd say that to the supervisor and at the toolbox meeting. That's our safety meeting before shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd figure I've got three years on the dragline, tops. I'd want to be out before the rush. But I'd also be thinking, out to where, if the robots are coming for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd pay off the truck and get the dentist sorted, so I've got no debts. I'd start putting in for the council plant operator jobs, graders and rollers on the roads, because that's local. And I'd keep sixty a week aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's there every day, but I'd have a plan, so I'd not be falling apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years give you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get the debts off me. That's the big one. If I go into whatever happens with no debts, I can live on not much. With two years I go in owing money, and that's the worst way to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't the council road machines get automated too, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, eventually. But councils are slow, they still do half their forms on paper. I'd bet on a council being the last place to get robots, and I'd be right, I think.

S3.say: We've got a few years, so the company should help people find other work now, not when the letters come. I'd say it at the safety meeting.
S3.think: I've got three years on the dragline at most and I'd want to be out before the rush. But out to where, if robots are coming for everyone?
S3.do: Clears his truck loan and dentist bill in the first year so he has no debts. Applies for local council road-machine operator jobs and saves sixty a week.
S3.feel: Anxious every day but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: I'd bet on a council being the last place to get robots, and I'd be right, I think.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Sam's priority is to be debt-free rather than to learn anything new. His choice of council work is a bet on slow-moving institutions, made with humour. He reads the mine closure and AI as two clocks running at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. By then Harlan's probably closed for coal reasons anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, nobody should be caught short in this one. If people are, it's because they didn't plan, or because the company didn't tell them. I'd say plan early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still drag my feet, because that's who I am. I'd keep running the dragline for as long as they'd let me. Then maybe five years in, I'd start looking, once I could see what was actually working for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the dragline and get the debts paid, then start saving properly. Around year five I'd look at the crane licence, because cranes on building sites might hang on a while. I'd watch what the people who left first ended up doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's still sad, but ten years is a long time. A lot can happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drag your feet. Do you think that's a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I know it is. Jess tells me that all the time, she's the one with the plan. But I've watched guys rush into things, solar panel courses and the like, and come out with nothing. I'd rather be second than wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Harlan to look like in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still there, with the pub and the football ground. Maybe with a few businesses that fix things or grow things. I don't need it to be big, I just need it to not be empty.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so nobody should be caught short; if they are, they didn't plan or weren't told. I'd say plan early.
S4.think: I'd still drag my feet, because that's who I am, and keep on the dragline as long as they'd let me. About five years in I'd look at what's working for others.
S4.do: Keeps running the dragline, pays off debts and then saves properly. Around year five considers a crane licence for building sites, after watching what earlier leavers ended up doing.
S4.feel: Uneasy and a bit sad, but ten years feels like a long time.
S4.quote: I don't need it to be big, I just need it to not be empty.
S4.fieldNote: Sam openly admits he'd delay, and accepts the risk because he's seen rushed retraining fail. His partner Jess is the planner in the house. His hopes for the town are small and specific: the pub, the sports ground, a few new businesses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is the company paying out properly and something to cover the rent for a year, so we're not straight onto my mum's couch. And a real job nearby, not a course in the city.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like to be good at something nobody needs. I'm one of the best on that dragline in the state, probably, and nobody outside Harlan would care. That's a funny thing to carry around.

headlineQuote: Maybe what it's like to be good at something nobody needs.
portrait: Sam Wagner is a 27-year-old dragline operator at a small coal mine, one of only three people who can run its forty-year-old machine, living with his hairdresser partner Jess on two weeks of savings. He never uses AI and prefers to let others test new things first. He's calm in the plateau, uneasy in steady disruption because he sees cheaper robot coal elsewhere closing his mine. Two-year AGI alarms him and sends him back to his parents' spare room, while five and ten years let him clear debts and aim for slow-changing council or crane work. He blames no one in particular and talks about company maths more than villains.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd still owe money and have no time to find other work.
whatWouldHelp: A proper company payout, a year of rent covered, and a real job nearby rather than a course in the city.
